title: Turkey
subtitle: 1923–1980 · The Single-Party Republic, the Democrat Decade, Coups and Coalitions, and the Years of Violence

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Atatürk and İnönü, the Democrat Party and Menderes, the officers of 1960, and the coalitions of the 1960s and 1970s

entries.label: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk
entries.hint: Mustafa Kemal was elected the first president of the Republic on 29 October 1923 and re-elected three times by the assembly until his death on 10 November 1938. He was also chairman of the Republican People's Party. The Surname Law of 1934 gave him the name Atatürk, 'father of the Turks'. The period is the era of his reforms, and of a single-party regime.
entries.note: TBMM records; Law no. 2587 (24 November 1934); Erik Zürcher, Turkey: A Modern History (1993); Andrew Mango, Atatürk (1999).

entries.label: İsmet İnönü
entries.hint: İnönü, Atatürk's long-serving prime minister, was elected president by the assembly the day after Atatürk's death and took the title Milli Şef, 'national chief'. He kept the country out of the Second World War until 1945, and in 1945–1946 oversaw the move to multiparty politics. He left office in May 1950 after the Democrat Party's victory.
entries.note: TBMM records; Zürcher 1993; Metin Heper, İsmet İnönü (1998).

entries.label: Celal Bayar
entries.hint: Bayar, a banker and Atatürk's last prime minister, founded the Democrat Party in 1946 and was elected president by the new assembly on 22 May 1950. He held the post, with Menderes as prime minister, until the coup of 27 May 1960. The Yassıada court sentenced him to death, a sentence commuted because of his age, and he was released in 1964.
entries.note: TBMM records; Zürcher 1993; Yassıada Supreme Court verdict (15 September 1961).

entries.label: Cemal Gürsel
entries.hint: General Cemal Gürsel, the commander of the land forces, led the National Unity Committee that took power on 27 May 1960 and was head of state, prime minister and minister of defence in the 1960–1961 interim. The assembly elected him president in October 1961, and he held the office until illness forced him from it in March 1966.
entries.note: National Unity Committee Law (12 June 1960); TBMM 26 October 1961; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Cevdet Sunay
entries.hint: General Cevdet Sunay, chief of the general staff, was chosen president in March 1966 on the army's wish as a candidate above party, and served the full term to 1973, through the memorandum of 1971. His term was a period of military guardianship.
entries.note: TBMM, 28 March 1966; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Fahri Korutürk
entries.hint: Admiral Fahri Korutürk, a former naval commander and ambassador, was elected on 6 April 1973 as a compromise after the parties refused the generals' candidate. In his term fell the Cyprus operation of 1974, the street violence of the late 1970s, and in the end the assembly's failure to elect a successor in 1980.
entries.note: TBMM records; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: İnönü's governments and the single party
entries.hint: İsmet İnönü was prime minister in 1923–1924 and again from 1925 to 1937, with a short interval under Fethi Okyar. His governments carried out the reforms, put down the revolts and, under the Law for the Maintenance of Order, closed the parties and the press. He resigned in 1937 after disagreements with Atatürk.
entries.note: Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999; TBMM records.

entries.label: Bayar, Saydam and Saracoğlu
entries.hint: Celal Bayar (1937–1939), Refik Saydam (1939–1942) and Şükrü Saracoğlu (1942–1946) led the governments of the late single-party period and the war years, with their neutral foreign policy, the wartime economy, the Wealth Tax and in 1945–1946 the decision to open the system to rival parties.
entries.note: Zürcher 1993; TBMM records.

entries.label: The transition cabinets
entries.hint: Recep Peker (1946–1947), Hasan Saka (1947–1949) and Şemsettin Günaltay (1949–1950) governed for the CHP while the Democrat Party grew as an opposition. The elections of 1946, with open voting and secret counting, were disputed, and those of May 1950 were free and ended the single-party rule.
entries.note: Law no. 5545 (electoral law, 1950); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Adnan Menderes
entries.hint: Adnan Menderes was prime minister for ten years under three election victories (1950, 1954, 1957). His governments pushed the countryside's roads, credit and tractors, brought Turkey into NATO and, after 1955, as the economy faltered, put limits on the press and the opposition. He was deposed in the coup of 27 May 1960, tried at Yassıada and hanged on 17 September 1961.
entries.note: TBMM records; Yassıada trials; Feroz Ahmad, The Turkish Experiment in Democracy (1977).

entries.label: The National Unity Committee and the İnönü coalitions
entries.hint: The military government of the National Unity Committee under Gürsel ruled until October 1961. After the elections of that year no party had a majority, and İnönü led three coalitions of the CHP with the Justice Party and smaller parties until February 1965, under the shadow of coup attempts by Talat Aydemir.
entries.note: Provisional constitutional law of the National Unity Committee (12 June 1960); election results (15 October 1961); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Süleyman Demirel and the Justice Party
entries.hint: The Justice Party, the heir of the Democrats, won the election of October 1965 outright and in 1969 again, and Süleyman Demirel was prime minister until 12 March 1971. His government built dams and roads, saw the new constitution's labour and press freedoms used by the left, and resigned when the military's memorandum came.
entries.note: Election results (10 October 1965, 12 October 1969); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The above-party governments
entries.hint: Following the memorandum, Nihat Erim (1971–1972), Ferit Melen and Naim Talu formed governments of technocrats and officers under military pressure, with martial law in the cities and the courts and the prosecution of the left, and constitutional amendments that restricted the freedoms of 1961.
entries.note: Constitutional amendments (September 1971, 1973); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The coalitions of Ecevit and Demirel
entries.hint: Bülent Ecevit's CHP won the election of 1973 and formed a government with Erbakan's National Salvation Party in January 1974 which ordered the Cyprus operation. In the years to 1980, no party had a majority: Demirel's 'nationalist front' coalitions alternated with Ecevit's governments (1977, 1978–1979), and an interim government, while the economy slid and violence rose. Demirel's last government was in office on 12 September 1980.
entries.note: Election results (14 October 1973, 5 June 1977); TBMM records; Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Kurdish revolts and Dersim, Korea, the pogrom of 1955, the coups and the Cyprus operations, and the street violence of the late 1970s

entries.label: Sheikh Said's rebellion
entries.hint: In February 1925 Sheikh Said of Palu, a Naqshbandi sheikh of the Zaza Kurds, led a rising in the east that combined religious grievance against the abolition of the caliphate with Kurdish national claims. It reached the edge of Diyarbakır and was put down by April with the use of the railway and aircraft. Sheikh Said and some forty followers were hanged at Diyarbakır on 29 June 1925, and the government used the revolt to pass the Law for the Maintenance of Order.
entries.note: Law no. 578 (4 March 1925); Independence Tribunal at Diyarbakır; Martin van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992); Robert Olson, The Emergence of Kurdish Nationalism (1989).

entries.label: The Ararat revolt and Zilan
entries.hint: The Kurdish nationalist league Khoybun organised from 1927 a rising in the Ararat region under İhsan Nuri, who held out with the help of the Iranian border. The army and air force attacked in the summer of 1930, and at Zilan in July many villagers were killed; the number of dead is disputed and runs from hundreds to many thousands. An exchange of border territory with Iran in 1932 gave Turkey the heights of Little Ararat.
entries.note: Turkish General Staff reports; Robert Olson, The Kurdish Nationalist Movement (1991); van Bruinessen 1992.

entries.label: The Thrace events
entries.hint: After the Settlement Law was passed in 1934, and following a press campaign, Jewish communities in the towns of Eastern Thrace suffered boycotts, threats, attacks and looting in June and July. Thousands of Jews left for Istanbul and elsewhere, and the government denied that it had been organised. The community's size in Thrace fell sharply.
entries.note: Rıfat Bali, Cumhuriyet Yıllarında Türkiye Yahudileri (1999); Corry Guttstadt, Turkey, the Jews, and the Holocaust (2013).

entries.label: Dersim
entries.hint: The government renamed Dersim 'Tunceli' by the law of 1935 and in 1937 sent the army against the Alevi Kurdish tribes of the mountains. Their leader Seyid Riza was hanged on 15 November 1937. The military operations and bombing of 1937–1938 killed, in an official document later cited by prime minister Erdoğan, some 13,800 people; other estimates run to several times that number, and thousands more were deported to the west. In 2011 Prime Minister Erdoğan apologised for it on behalf of the state.
entries.note: Tunceli Law no. 2884 (25 December 1935); General Staff reports; Erdoğan's speech (23 November 2011); Martin van Bruinessen, 'Genocide in Kurdistan?' (1994); Hans-Lukas Kieser (ed.), Turkey Beyond Nationalism (2006).

entries.label: The Turkish brigade in Korea
entries.hint: The Menderes government sent a brigade of about 5,000 men to the United Nations command in Korea in October 1950, in the first Turkish commitment to a Western-led war. It fought at Kunuri in November 1950, covering the retreat of the American forces, and at Wawon; some 740 Turkish soldiers died in the war. The commitment helped win NATO membership in 1952.
entries.note: Turkish General Staff, Kore Harbi; Zürcher 1993; Edward Erickson on Kunuri; TBMM resolution (25 July 1950).

entries.label: The Istanbul pogrom of 6–7 September 1955
entries.hint: After a false report that Atatürk's birthplace in Salonica had been bombed, crowds organised in Istanbul on the night of 6 September 1955 attacked the shops, houses, churches and schools of the Greek community and of Armenians and Jews. Thousands of shops and houses and dozens of churches were damaged, and the dead are given as between about a dozen and some thirty. The government blamed communists; later courts and historians pointed to an organisation within the state's own services, and the Greek community of Istanbul, which had numbered about 100,000, dwindled after it.
entries.note: Speros Vryonis, The Mechanism of Catastrophe (2005); Dilek Güven, Cumhuriyet Dönemi Azınlık Politikaları ve Stratejileri Bağlamında 6–7 Eylül Olayları (2005); Yassıada trial records.

entries.label: The coup of 27 May 1960
entries.hint: In the small hours of 27 May 1960, a group of officers around General Cemal Gürsel seized Ankara and arrested the president, the prime minister, the ministers and the Democrat deputies, in the first coup of the Republic. They acted after months of student demonstrations, the closing of the opposition's activity and the establishment of an investigative committee. The military's National Unity Committee ruled for about seventeen months.
entries.note: Proclamation of 27 May 1960; Law no. 1 of the National Unity Committee; William Hale, Turkish Politics and the Military (1994); George Harris, 'The Role of the Military in Turkish Politics' (1965).

entries.label: The Aydemir attempts
entries.hint: Colonel Talat Aydemir, an officer who had taken part in the 1960 coup and was then retired, led an attempt on 22 February 1962 and a second on 20–21 May 1963, both aimed at replacing the civilian coalition with a military regime. Both failed, and Aydemir was executed on 5 July 1964 with another officer. The attempts left the civilian governments fearful of the army.
entries.note: Hale 1994; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Cyprus, 1963–1964
entries.hint: Violence between Greek and Turkish Cypriots began in Nicosia on 21 December 1963, after Archbishop Makarios proposed amendments to the 1960 constitution. Turkish Cypriots withdrew into enclaves and the Greek Cypriots held the state. In August 1964 Turkish aircraft bombed Greek Cypriot positions at Tillyria after attacks on Kokkina. A UN force was sent in March 1964, and İnönü's plan to intervene was stopped by President Johnson's letter of 5 June 1964.
entries.note: Treaty of Guarantee (1960); UN Security Council res. 186 (4 March 1964); Johnson letter (5 June 1964); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The memorandum of 12 March 1971
entries.hint: After a year of strikes, kidnappings, bank robberies and student demonstrations, the chief of the general staff and the commanders of the services delivered a memorandum to the president on 12 March 1971 demanding a government that would carry out the reforms and stop anarchy, or the army would take power. Demirel resigned the same day, and in April martial law was declared in eleven provinces.
entries.note: Memorandum of 12 March 1971 (TRT broadcast); Hale 1994; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Gezmiş and the guerrillas
entries.hint: Small groups of the revolutionary left, among them Deniz Gezmiş's People's Liberation Army and the Turkish People's Liberation Party-Front, carried out robberies and kidnappings of American personnel and Turkish officials in 1971–1972. At Kızıldere in March 1972 Mahir Çayan and nine comrades were killed by soldiers, and the three NATO technicians they held hostage also died; Gezmiş and two comrades were hanged on 6 May 1972.
entries.note: Martial law court records; Zürcher 1993; Feroz Ahmad, The Making of Modern Turkey (1993).

entries.label: The Cyprus operation of 1974
entries.hint: After the Greek junta's National Guard overthrew Archbishop Makarios on 15 July 1974, Turkey landed troops near Kyrenia on 20 July, citing its rights as a guarantor under the 1960 treaty, and in a second phase in August took about 37 per cent of the island. Turkish and Turkish Cypriot sources call it a peace operation and a lawful intervention; Greek Cypriots, Greece and most governments term it an invasion and continuing occupation, while UN resolutions called for the withdrawal of foreign forces and respect for Cyprus's sovereignty. About 160,000 Greek Cypriots fled the north and some 45,000 Turkish Cypriots moved to it; some 1,500 Greek Cypriots and about 500 Turkish Cypriots are listed as missing for 1963–1974. As of 2026 the island is still divided.
entries.note: Treaty of Guarantee, art. IV (1960); UNSC res. 353 (20 July 1974); UNGA res. 3212 (1974); Committee on Missing Persons in Cyprus; William Mallinson, Cyprus: A Modern History (2005).

entries.label: The street violence of 1976–1980
entries.hint: Between 1976 and the coup of September 1980, clashes between left- and right-wing militants, assassinations of politicians, journalists and teachers, and bombings killed, by the figures usually quoted, about 5,000 people or more, in the last months some twenty a day. Universities, neighbourhoods and the police were divided, and the parties of the coalition governments were unable to act. It formed the background of the military's seizure of power.
entries.note: General Staff and Interior Ministry statistics; Zürcher 1993; Hale 1994.

entries.label: The May Day massacre of 1977
entries.hint: During the trade-union confederation DİSK's May Day rally at Taksim Square in Istanbul on 1 May 1977, shots were fired into the crowd from surrounding buildings and a panic followed; at least 34 people were killed, many of them in the crush, and hundreds injured. Who fired the shots, and with what purpose, is still disputed.
entries.note: DİSK report (1977); Istanbul martial law prosecutor; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Maraş and Çorum
entries.hint: In Kahramanmaraş in December 1978, after the murder of two left-wing teachers, nationalist militants incited crowds to attack the Alevi quarters; the official toll was 111 dead and hundreds injured, and martial law was declared. In Çorum in May and July 1980 similar violence killed dozens, again mostly Alevis. Both are remembered by the Alevi communities.
entries.note: Martial law prosecutors' indictments; Zürcher 1993; Elise Massicard, The Alevis in Turkey and Europe (2013).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The abolition of the caliphate, the Civil Code, the alphabet and women's vote, the multiparty transition, and the constitution of 1961

entries.label: The abolition of the caliphate
entries.hint: On 3 March 1924 the Grand National Assembly abolished the caliphate, expelled the Ottoman dynasty, abolished the Ministry of the Sharia and Pious Foundations, and with the Law of Unification of Education placed all schools under the Ministry of Education. A Directorate of Religious Affairs, under the prime minister, was set up to run the mosques.
entries.note: Laws nos. 430, 431 and 429 (3 March 1924); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The constitution of 1924
entries.hint: The constitution of 20 April 1924 declared that sovereignty belongs to the nation, concentrated power in the assembly, and made Islam the state religion until the amendment of 1928 removed the clause. It remained in force, with the amendments of 1937 which added the six principles, until the coup of 1960.
entries.note: Teşkilât-ı Esasiye Kanunu, no. 491 (20 April 1924); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Hat Law and the closing of the lodges
entries.hint: The Hat Law of 25 November 1925 made the brimmed hat the required headgear for men, in place of the fez and turban, and five days later the assembly closed all the dervish lodges and tombs and banned the titles of sheikh and dervish. Resistance in Erzurum, Rize and Sivas was put down by the Independence Tribunals, with executions.
entries.note: Law no. 671 (25 November 1925); Law no. 677 (30 November 1925); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Civil Code
entries.hint: The assembly adopted on 17 February 1926 a civil code taken almost entire from the Swiss code, and the Code of Obligations and Commercial Code from Switzerland and Italy's and Germany's models. It abolished polygamy and Islamic marriage law, gave men and women equal divorce rights and equal inheritance, and came into force on 4 October 1926.
entries.note: Law no. 743 (17 February 1926), Medeni Kanun; Zürcher 1993; Deniz Kandiyoti (ed.), Women, Islam and the State (1991).

entries.label: The alphabet reform
entries.hint: Mustafa Kemal presented the new Latin alphabet to the public in Istanbul in August 1928, and the law of 1 November 1928 made its use compulsory in all public documents and in the press from the end of the year. National schools were opened to teach it. Literacy, which was about 10 per cent in 1927, rose slowly.
entries.note: Law no. 1353 (1 November 1928); Geoffrey Lewis, The Turkish Language Reform (1999).

entries.label: The Settlement Law and the Surname Law
entries.hint: The Settlement Law of June 1934 (no. 2510) allowed the government to settle people by cultural and linguistic affinity, and to resettle those in regions whose population it wished to Turkify, among them Kurdish districts. The Surname Law of 21 June 1934 (no. 2525) obliged every citizen to take a Turkish surname and abolished the titles of aga, bey and pasha.
entries.note: Law no. 2510 (14 June 1934); Law no. 2525 (21 June 1934); Soner Çağaptay, Islam, Secularism and Nationalism in Modern Turkey (2006).

entries.label: Women's suffrage
entries.hint: Women were given the right to vote in municipal elections in 1930 and in national elections and to stand for the assembly by the constitutional amendment of 5 December 1934, earlier than in France or Italy. In the 1935 election eighteen women were elected to the assembly. The assembly was a single-party body, in which the vote did not decide the government.
entries.note: Law no. 2599 (5 December 1934); Zürcher 1993; Kandiyoti 1991.

entries.label: The six principles in the constitution
entries.hint: The amendment of 5 February 1937 wrote the party's six 'arrows' — republicanism, nationalism, populism, etatism, secularism and revolutionism — into the constitution, and defined the state as secular for the first time. The constitution had also lost its Islamic clause in 1928.
entries.note: Law no. 3115 (5 February 1937); CHP programme of 1931 and 1935.

entries.label: The Wealth Tax
entries.hint: The Wealth Tax law of 11 November 1942, passed to take in war profits and pay for the army's mobilisation, was applied by local committees without appeal, and the rates for non-Muslims, among them Armenians, Greeks and Jews, were often several times those of Muslims. Those who could not pay had their goods sold, and over a thousand, all non-Muslim, were sent to labour camps at Aşkale; some died. The tax was cancelled on 15 March 1944 and the camps closed.
entries.note: Law no. 4305 (11 November 1942); Law no. 4530 (15 March 1944); Ayhan Aktar, Varlık Vergisi ve 'Türkleştirme' Politikaları (2000); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The move to the multiparty system
entries.hint: In 1945, as the war ended and Turkey sought a place among the western states, İnönü announced that the opposition would be tolerated. The Democrat Party was founded in January 1946, the election of July 1946 was held with open voting and secret counting, and in 1950 a new electoral law gave secret ballots and judicial supervision. The DP won 408 of 487 seats on 14 May 1950, the first peaceful change of government in the Republic.
entries.note: Law no. 5545 (16 February 1950); election results (14 May 1950); Feroz Ahmad 1977.

entries.label: The Yassıada trials
entries.hint: After the coup of 1960, the Democrat leaders and several hundred former ministers, deputies and officials were tried on Yassıada island by a court of the military regime; the charges included violating the constitution, corruption and the events of September 1955. Bayar, Menderes and some dozen others were sentenced to death in September 1961; most sentences were commuted, but Menderes, with Zorlu and Polatkan, was hanged. The trials remained a point of division between the heirs of the DP and the army.
entries.note: Yassıada Supreme Court verdict (15 September 1961); Hale 1994; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The State Planning Organisation
entries.hint: The military government set up the State Planning Organisation in September 1960, and the constitution of 1961 made planned development a duty of the state. Five-year plans, binding on the public sector and indicative for the private, were drawn from 1963, with import substitution at the centre.
entries.note: Law no. 91 (30 September 1960); First Five-Year Development Plan (1963–1967); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The constitution of 1961
entries.hint: A constituent assembly in which the army's National Unity Committee, the CHP and professional bodies sat, but not the banned Democrats, wrote the constitution of 1961, which set up a senate, a constitutional court, proportional representation, a right to strike and academic and press freedom, and a National Security Council. It was approved in a referendum on 9 July 1961 by about 62 per cent of voters.
entries.note: Constitution no. 334 (9 July 1961); Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The secular reforms and their reversal, the Nur movement, the Alevi villages and the rise of political Islam

entries.label: The Alevi communities
entries.hint: Alevi villages in central and eastern Anatolia were officially counted as Muslims, without a state office for their religion or recognition of their houses of prayer, and the dervish lodges that housed them were closed in 1925. Many Alevis supported the Kemalist reforms and later the left. The violence in Maraş and Çorum in 1978–1980 made the Alevi question a political one.
entries.note: Massicard 2013; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Nur movement
entries.hint: Said Nursi, a Kurdish scholar who was exiled to Barla in 1926, wrote there the Risale-i Nur, a commentary on the Qur'an. His writings were copied by hand and spread through the country as a pietist, non-political movement. He was tried and imprisoned in 1935, 1943–1944 and 1948–1949, and acquitted more than once; he died in 1960.
entries.note: Şerif Mardin, Religion and Social Change in Modern Turkey (1989); court records at Eskişehir (1935).

entries.label: The Arabic call to prayer
entries.hint: From January 1932 the call to prayer was given in Turkish in the mosques, and a law of 1941 forbade the Arabic. After the elections of 1950, the Democrat Party's first act in religious matters was to restore it, on 16 June 1950. The question stood for the two sides' views on the place of religion in the state.
entries.note: Law of 1941 on the call to prayer; Law no. 5665 (16 June 1950); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Erbakan and the National Salvation Party
entries.hint: Necmettin Erbakan, an engineer from Konya, founded the National Order Party in January 1970; it was closed by the Constitutional Court after the memorandum, and he refounded it as the National Salvation Party in 1972. The party won 48 seats in 1973 and 24 in 1977 and was a partner in coalitions in 1974 and 1975–1977. It was the first mass party of political Islam in the Republic.
entries.note: Constitutional Court decision (May 1971); election results (1973, 1977); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Halki seminary
entries.hint: The Greek Orthodox Theological School of Halki, founded in 1844 on Heybeliada, was closed in 1971 when the state took over private higher education. It had trained the clergy of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, and its closing, which left the Patriarchate without an institution for its clergy in Turkey, remains a standing complaint.
entries.note: Constitutional Court decision of 1971 on private higher education; Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Hagia Sophia as a museum, Nâzım Hikmet in prison, İnce Memed and Yeşilçam

entries.label: Hagia Sophia as a museum
entries.hint: A cabinet decree of 24 November 1934, signed by Atatürk, converted Hagia Sophia from a mosque into a museum, and the uncovering of its mosaics began with American and Byzantine Institute teams. The building stayed a museum for 86 years, until it was returned to use as a mosque by a decision of July 2020.
entries.note: Council of Ministers decree no. 2/1589 (24 November 1934); Council of State ruling (10 July 2020).

entries.label: Nâzım Hikmet in prison
entries.hint: The poet Nâzım Hikmet, a communist who had worked in Moscow in the 1920s, was sentenced in 1938 to some 28 years for inciting the navy to revolt and spent twelve years in prison, writing his epic Human Landscapes from My Country there. He was freed in the amnesty of 1950, left for the Soviet Union in 1951 and was stripped of citizenship; he died in Moscow in 1963.
entries.note: Nâzım Hikmet, Memleketimden İnsan Manzaraları (written 1941–1945); Council of Ministers decision of 25 July 1951; Blasing, Nâzim Hikmet: The Life and Times of Turkey's World-Famous Poet (2013).

entries.label: The Garip poets
entries.hint: Orhan Veli Kanık, Oktay Rifat and Melih Cevdet Anday published their volume Garip in 1941 with a preface rejecting rhyme, metre and poetic diction for the speech of the street and the 'ordinary man'. The Garip movement changed Turkish poetry. Orhan Veli died in 1950 at 36.
entries.note: Garip (1941), with Orhan Veli's preface.

entries.label: Anıtkabir
entries.hint: The mausoleum of Atatürk, designed by Emin Onat and Orhan Arda after an international competition of 1941 and built on a hill in Ankara, was finished in 1953, and his coffin was moved there on 10 November 1953 from the Ethnography Museum. It combines the forms of Hittite sculpture and of classical architecture, and is the national shrine.
entries.note: Anıtkabir competition (1941–1942); inauguration of 10 November 1953; Bozdoğan, Modernism and Nation Building (2001).

entries.label: Yeşilçam
entries.hint: The Turkish film industry, centred in the Yeşilçam street in Beyoğlu, grew from a few films a year in the 1940s to more than 200 a year in the early 1970s, one of the most productive in the world, making melodramas, comedies, adventure films and, after 1960, social-realist films. The directors Yılmaz Güney and Metin Erksan made some of its most important work.
entries.note: Nijat Özön, Türk Sineması Kronolojisi (1960); Giovanni Scognamillo, Türk Sinema Tarihi (1987).

entries.label: İnce Memed
entries.hint: Yaşar Kemal, a Kurdish-born writer from the Çukurova, published in 1955 İnce Memed, the novel of a young peasant's flight into the mountains from an oppressive landlord. It was translated into dozens of languages and made him the best-known Turkish writer abroad. It is the story of the agha and the bandit in the plain that was being mechanised.
entries.note: Yaşar Kemal, İnce Memed (1955); Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Turkish History Thesis, the Village Institutes, the translation bureau and the Turkish left

entries.label: The Turkish History Thesis and the Sun Language Theory
entries.hint: The Turkish Historical Society (1931) and the Turkish Language Society (1932) propagated a view that the Turks had been the carriers of civilisation from Central Asia to the Hittites and Sumerians, and that all languages derived from an original Turkish, the 'Sun Language Theory' of 1935–1936. The first congresses were held in 1932. Both theses were quietly dropped after Atatürk's death.
entries.note: Türk Tarihinin Ana Hatları (1930); First Turkish History Congress (July 1932); Turkish Language Congress (September 1932); Büşra Ersanlı, İktidar ve Tarih (1992).

entries.label: The Village Institutes
entries.hint: The Village Institutes, founded by law in April 1940 under the minister Hasan Âli Yücel and the educator İsmail Hakkı Tonguç, took village boys and girls in boarding schools which taught teaching with farming, building and crafts. About 17,000 teachers graduated from the twenty-odd institutes. They were turned into ordinary teachers' schools by the Democrat government in 1954, and are remembered as the republic's most original education experiment.
entries.note: Law no. 3803 (17 April 1940); Law no. 6234 (1954); Fay Kirby, Türkiye'de Köy Enstitüleri (1962).

entries.label: The Translation Bureau
entries.hint: Under the minister of education Hasan Âli Yücel, the Translation Bureau (1940) and the Translation Office, working with the Education Ministry, translated hundreds of works, among them the Greek and Latin classics, Shakespeare, Cervantes, Goethe, Dostoevsky and the philosophers into Turkish, in what was the largest translation programme of the Republic. The programme lost its momentum after Yücel left office in 1946 and was wound down in the following decades.
entries.note: Tercüme Bürosu (1940); Hasan Âli Yücel, Maarif Vekili; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Workers' Party of Turkey and Yön
entries.hint: The Workers' Party of Turkey, founded in 1961 by trade unionists and entered into the assembly in 1965 with 15 seats, was the first socialist party in parliament, and the weekly Yön (1961–1967) of Doğan Avcıoğlu argued for a non-capitalist 'national democratic revolution'. The party was closed in 1971 after the memorandum.
entries.note: Yön (1961–1967); election results (1965); Constitutional Court decision (20 July 1971); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Turkish-Islamic synthesis
entries.hint: The Intellectuals' Hearth, founded in 1970 by conservative academics and writers, argued that the national culture of Turkey was the Turkish and Islamic heritage together, in opposition to the left, and its idea of the 'Turkish-Islamic synthesis' was adopted after 1980 as a state policy in the schools.
entries.note: Aydınlar Ocağı (1970), Kültür Raporu; Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The abolition of the tithe, etatism and planning, the agricultural boom, the guest workers and the crisis of 1977–1980

entries.label: The abolition of the tithe
entries.hint: The assembly abolished the tithe (aşar), the one-tenth levy on the harvest which had been the main tax on the peasantry since Ottoman times, on 17 February 1925. It was replaced by a land tax and by a tax on livestock, and the state lost a large share, about a quarter, of its revenue.
entries.note: Law no. 552 (17 February 1925); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Etatism and the first Five-Year Plan
entries.hint: After the world depression the state took the lead in industry: Sümerbank was founded in 1933, a first Five-Year Industrial Plan (1934–1938), drawn up with Soviet advice and credit, built textile, sugar, paper and iron plants, and the state took over the foreign-owned railways and ports. Etatism was one of the six principles of 1937.
entries.note: First Five-Year Industrial Plan (1934); Sümerbank Law no. 2262 (1933); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The agricultural boom of the 1950s
entries.hint: Marshall Plan credits, tractors, roads and farm loans, and the Korean War demand brought a boom: tractors increased from about 1,750 in 1948 to tens of thousands by the late 1950s, the area under crops expanded by a half, and wheat exports rose. Growth fell away from 1954, and inflation, import shortages and debts followed.
entries.note: State Institute of Statistics; Marshall Plan records; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The 1958 stabilisation programme
entries.hint: In August 1958, with foreign exchange exhausted and debts unpaid, the government agreed with the IMF and the OEEC on a stabilisation programme which devalued the lira from 2.80 to 9 to the dollar, and rescheduled foreign debts. It was the first of the IMF packages.
entries.note: Decree of 4 August 1958; IMF agreement; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The guest workers and their remittances
entries.hint: The agreement for the recruitment of labour signed by Turkey and West Germany on 30 October 1961, followed by agreements with Austria, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, sent some 700,000 Turkish workers to West Germany and hundreds of thousands more to other countries by the time Germany stopped recruitment in November 1973. Their remittances became a main source of foreign exchange and, until 1973, helped pay for the import-substitution model.
entries.note: Anwerbeabkommen (30 October 1961); Turkish Employment Service data; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Planned import substitution
entries.hint: Under the five-year plans the economy grew at about 6 per cent a year in 1963–1977, behind high tariffs and import quotas and with state banks and the public enterprises; the home market was supplied by new car, white-goods and chemicals industries, in which the Koç and Sabancı holdings grew. The model depended on imported oil and machinery and ended in a balance-of-payments crisis.
entries.note: State Planning Organisation plans (1963–1977); Zürcher 1993; Pamuk 2000.

entries.label: The crisis of 1977–1980 and the decisions of 24 January
entries.hint: After the oil price rise of 1973 and the arms embargo, Turkey ran balance-of-payments deficits, financed by short-term credit; by 1977 the debt could not be paid, and in 1978–1980 there were shortages of fuel and goods and inflation approaching or above 100 per cent. On 24 January 1980 Demirel's government, with Turgut Özal as its architect, announced a stabilisation and liberalisation programme worked out with the IMF, which was applied after the coup of September.
entries.note: Decisions of 24 January 1980; IMF stand-by agreement (1979–1980); Zürcher 1993; Pamuk 2000.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The railways, Karabük, the Bosphorus Bridge and television

entries.label: The railway-building programme
entries.hint: The Republic nationalised the foreign-owned railways and built about 3,000 kilometres of new line, mainly state-financed and carried through the interior, among them Ankara–Sivas (1930), Sivas–Erzurum and the lines to the coal of Zonguldak and the copper of Ergani. The network grew by some 80 per cent by 1950.
entries.note: Turkish State Railways (TCDD) records; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Radio and television
entries.hint: Radio broadcasting began from Istanbul in 1927 and the State Radio at Ankara in 1938; the state broadcaster TRT was set up by the constitution of 1961 and the law of 1964, and began television in 1968. The constitution guaranteed the broadcaster's autonomy.
entries.note: Law no. 359 (1964); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Karabük iron and steel works
entries.hint: The Karabük works, built with British (Brassert) design and finance from 1937 and opened in 1939 in a village in the Black Sea mountains, were the first integrated iron and steel works in Turkey and produced steel for the railways and military. The town of Karabük grew round it.
entries.note: Karabük İktisadi Devlet Teşekkülü records; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Bosphorus Bridge
entries.hint: The Bosphorus Bridge, a suspension bridge of 1,074 metres' main span designed by Freeman Fox and Partners and built by a British–German consortium from 1970, was opened on 30 October 1973, at the fiftieth anniversary of the Republic, as the first fixed link between Europe and Asia.
entries.note: Bosphorus Bridge records (Karayolları); opening of 30 October 1973.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Montreux, the war years, NATO, the Ankara Agreement and the arms embargo

entries.label: The Montreux Convention
entries.hint: The Montreux Convention of 20 July 1936 returned to Turkey the right to fortify and control the Straits, which Lausanne had demilitarised, while preserving free passage for merchant ships in peacetime and restricting the passage of warships of non-Black Sea powers. It remains in force.
entries.note: Convention regarding the Regime of the Straits (20 July 1936).

entries.label: The Hatay question
entries.hint: The sanjak of Alexandretta, under the French Mandate for Syria, was given autonomy in 1937 and in September 1938 proclaimed a Republic of Hatay; a Turkish military presence and elections of the same year gave the Turkish list a majority. The Hatay assembly voted for union on 29 June 1939 and the territory was annexed by Turkey. Syria did not recognise the loss.
entries.note: Franco-Turkish agreement of 23 June 1939; Hatay Assembly decision (29 June 1939); Sarah Shields, Fezzes in the River (2011).

entries.label: Neutrality in the Second World War
entries.hint: Turkey signed a treaty of mutual assistance with Britain and France in October 1939 but, after the fall of France, kept to neutrality and signed a friendship pact with Germany on 18 June 1941. It sold chrome to both sides and under allied pressure it broke off relations with Germany in August 1944, and declared war in February 1945 to join the United Nations conference.
entries.note: Anglo-Franco-Turkish treaty (19 October 1939); German–Turkish treaty (18 June 1941); Zürcher 1993; Selim Deringil, Turkish Foreign Policy during the Second World War (1989).

entries.label: The Truman Doctrine and NATO
entries.hint: After Soviet demands in 1945–1946 for bases on the Straits and the return of Kars and Ardahan, the United States, in the Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947, extended military and economic aid to Turkey and Greece. Turkey sent troops to Korea in 1950 and joined NATO on 18 February 1952, a membership which has lasted since.
entries.note: Truman Doctrine (12 March 1947); Protocol of accession (18 February 1952); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The Ankara Agreement with the EEC
entries.hint: The association agreement of 12 September 1963 between Turkey and the European Economic Community provided for a customs union in stages and held out the prospect of full membership. It entered into force on 1 December 1964, and an additional protocol was signed in 1970.
entries.note: Ankara Agreement (12 September 1963); Additional Protocol (23 November 1970).

entries.label: The Johnson letter and the arms embargo
entries.hint: President Johnson's letter of 5 June 1964 warned İnönü that NATO might not defend Turkey if an operation in Cyprus brought Soviet intervention, and that American weapons could not be used there without consent. After the Cyprus operation of 1974 the US Congress imposed an arms embargo on Turkey in February 1975, lifted in September 1978. Turkey's relations with the United States and with the Soviet Union were reconsidered.
entries.note: Johnson letter (5 June 1964); Foreign Assistance Act amendment (December 1974, effective 5 February 1975); Zürcher 1993.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Erzincan earthquake, the census and the new cities, and the decline of the minorities

entries.label: The decline of the minorities
entries.hint: The non-Muslim communities of Turkey, which Lausanne protected, declined steadily: the Wealth Tax of 1942, the emigration of tens of thousands of Jews to Israel after 1948, the pogrom of 1955 and the expulsion of about 12,000 Greek citizens in 1964, with their families, drove most of the Greeks of Istanbul and a large part of the Jews and Armenians to leave. The Greek community, which numbered over 100,000 in 1923, was under ten thousand by 1980.
entries.note: Census data; Rıfat Bali; Alexis Alexandris, The Greek Minority of Istanbul and Greek-Turkish Relations 1918–1974 (1983).

entries.label: The population explosion
entries.hint: The first census of the Republic in 1927 counted 13.6 million people; by 1980 the census counted 44.7 million. The growth of 2 to 3 per cent a year was the result of falling mortality, with the end of epidemic and war, and sustained high fertility. The share of the population in towns rose from about a quarter to over 40 per cent.
entries.note: State Institute of Statistics, Census of 1927 and of 1980.

entries.label: The Erzincan earthquake
entries.hint: An earthquake of magnitude about 7.8 on the North Anatolian Fault in the night of 26–27 December 1939 destroyed Erzincan and other towns of the east in a snowy winter, and killed about 33,000 people. It was the deadliest of the Republic's earthquakes until 1999 and led to the first building regulations and to the Disaster Law of 1944.
entries.note: Seismological records; Law no. 4623 (1944); Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Migration to the cities
entries.hint: The mechanisation of farming and the new roads displaced millions of villagers, and the population of Istanbul grew from 1 million in 1950 to over 2.5 million in 1975, and that of Ankara more than fourfold. Newcomers built their own houses overnight on public land, the gecekondu, and in 1966 a law recognised them.
entries.note: Gecekondu Law no. 775 (1966); census data 1950–1980.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The vote and the surname, the gecekondu, the worker and the student, the Kurdish villager and the migrant in Germany

entries.label: The Kurdish villagers and the ban on Kurdish
entries.hint: Kurdish villages of the east were administered under the Reform Plan for the East (1925), by inspectors-general (1927–1952) and, in Dersim, under the Tunceli Law; Kurdish names, places and publications were forbidden, the Kurdish language was banned from schools and public use, and the Settlement Law allowed dispersal. Kurdish was spoken at home by millions, and the existence of a Kurdish people was officially denied; Kurdish cultural organisations appeared again in the 1960s.
entries.note: Reform Plan for the East (1925); Settlement Law (1934); van Bruinessen 1992; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: Women in the new republic
entries.hint: Women were elected to the assembly in 1935 (18 of 395), became judges and lawyers, and entered the professions and universities; Sabiha Gökçen, Atatürk's adopted daughter, became in 1936 the first Turkish woman pilot. The reforms affected women of the cities more than those of villages, where the civil code was often ignored.
entries.note: Election of 1935; Kandiyoti 1991; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The gecekondu
entries.hint: Migrants built their houses at night on land that was not theirs, since a house with a roof by dawn could not be torn down under custom, and the neighbourhoods grew into whole districts without water, sewers or title deeds. By 1980, by common estimates, perhaps two-fifths or more of Istanbul's people and over half of Ankara's lived in them. Their votes were courted by every party, and they were the base of the left and of the Islamic parties.
entries.note: Gecekondu Law no. 775 (1966); Kemal Karpat, The Gecekondu (1976).

entries.label: The generation of 1968
entries.hint: Students at Ankara, Istanbul and the Middle East Technical University, many from poor families of the provinces, organised in the Federation of Revolutionary Youth (Dev-Genç) from 1969, occupied faculties, demonstrated against the American Sixth Fleet and against the government, and were attacked by right-wing groups. The movement was broken by the memorandum of 1971; its leaders were imprisoned or killed.
entries.note: Dev-Genç records; Zürcher 1993; Feroz Ahmad, The Making of Modern Turkey (1993).

entries.label: The Turkish migrant in Germany
entries.hint: The 'guest workers' were recruited for factories, mines and construction, housed in hostels, and expected to return within a few years; many stayed, and in the late 1970s were joined by their families. The Turkish population of Germany reached more than a million by 1980, and its cultural and political lives began to interact with those of the home country.
entries.note: German Federal Statistical Office; Zürcher 1993.

entries.label: The workers of June 1970
entries.hint: When the government proposed in June 1970 to restrict the unions of the DİSK confederation, some 75,000 workers or more marched on 15 and 16 June in Istanbul and Kocaeli in the largest labour demonstration of the Republic to that date; martial law was declared and several people were killed. The law was later annulled by the Constitutional Court.
entries.note: Law no. 1317 (1970), later annulled by the Constitutional Court; Zürcher 1993.
